wstep: This card describes citrus salt made from lemon zest and salt, dried in the air, in a dehydrator or in the oven, following two UC Master Food Preserver handouts.

akapity: According to the Sacramento County UCCE Master Food Preservers, use 1 cup of flake or coarse salt and 3 tablespoons of citrus zest; a US cup holds about 237 ml.
Zest only the coloured outer peel and avoid the white pith.
Work the zest into the salt with your fingers, then spread the mixture on a baking tray.
Air-dry the mixture until it is completely dry, which takes 8 hours to overnight (UCCE Sacramento).
According to the UC ANR handout, the salt can also be dried in a dehydrator at 125 °F (about 52 °C) or in a 220 °F (105 °C) oven.
The salt is done when the zest feels dry and crumbles when pinched.
Pack only the completely cooled salt: warm dried food sweats, and that moisture can be enough for mould to grow.
Store the salt in clean, labelled jars; an optional desiccant pack helps keep it dry.
Packaging must be food grade: do not use trash bags or plastic or fibreboard containers that previously held non-food items.
Keep the jar airtight at room temperature for up to 2 months (UCCE Sacramento).
Store the jar in a cool, dry, dark place.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): the UC ANR handout gives the salt its best flavour in the first 3 months, and this card gives the shorter limit of 2 months.
Check the salt often (glass shows condensation); if it has taken up moisture but is not spoiled, use it at once or dry it again and repack it.
Throw away mouldy salt; also throw away salt that smells off.
